observed-data.t: We observed **H H T H H**. This data is now **fixed**. The question: which value of p would have made exactly this result **the most likely**?

candidate-low.t: Score a candidate flip by flip. Each head contributes **p**, each tail **1 − p**. For p = 0.2 the chips are **0.2, 0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 0.2**, and their product, the **likelihood, is only 0.0013**.

candidate-middle.t: For p = 0.5 every flip contributes 0.5, so the likelihood is **0.5⁵ = 0.031**. That is much better than 0.0013.

candidate-high.t: For p = 0.8 the chips are **0.8, 0.8, 0.2, 0.8, 0.8** and the likelihood is **0.082**, the best of the three. Under p = 0.8 the data we saw is **64 times more likely** than under p = 0.2.

likelihood-curve.t: Try every value of p from 0 to 1 and plot its likelihood: **L(p) = p⁴(1 − p)**. The three candidates are points on this curve, which **rises, peaks and falls**.

maximum.t: The top of the curve is where the data are **most likely**. It sits at **p = 0.8**. The data stayed fixed; only the parameter was varied.

mle.t: **p_MLE = argmax L(p) = 0.8.** “Argmax” means the value of p that gives the largest L. Here it equals **4/5**, the observed fraction of heads.

ml-connection.t: Fitting a probabilistic model usually means **maximum likelihood**: choose the parameters that make the training data most likely. We usually maximize the **log** of the likelihood, which has the same peak.
